Variable selection

Source: vignettes/variable-selection.Rmd
variable-selection.Rmd
library(bsfa)
set.seed(1234)

The problem

A frontier is usually written down with every regressor to hand, and the ones that turn out not to belong are then argued away from a table of credible bands: this one covers zero, drop it, refit. That reads one coefficient at a time, and it leaves the efficiency scores conditioned on whichever frontier the argument happened to settle on, with none of the uncertainty about that choice anywhere in the answer.

Variable selection puts the choice inside the sampler instead. An inclusion indicator is drawn for each candidate regressor in every sweep, so the posterior covers the frontiers as well as the coefficients, and the efficiency scores come out averaged over them.

bsfa offers the two algorithms of the bvartools package, the stochastic search variable selection of George, Sun and Ni (2008) and the Bayesian variable selection of Korobilis (2013). They differ in what an inclusion indicator does, which is the subject of most of this vignette, but they are used in exactly the same way.

The common interface

Both are switched on with the varsel argument of the constructor, and both take their prior from the varsel argument of add_priors(), which a model created with an algorithm requires and every other model refuses:

model <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, varsel = "ssvs")
model <- add_priors(model, varsel = list(...))

The draws of the indicators land in model$posterior$inclusion, one column per candidate, and their means are reported by summary() as PIP, the posterior probability that the regressor belongs in the frontier. Everything else about the model is unchanged: the same constructors, the same priors on the inefficiency term and the error, the same efficiency(), plot() and selection_criteria().

Data with something to drop

Two of the four regressors below have nothing to do with the frontier. A selection that works should keep x1 and x2 and discard z1 and z2.

d <- sim_sf(n = 400, beta = c(1, 0.5, 0.3), sigma_v = 0.2, par_u = 4)
d$z1 <- rnorm(nrow(d))
d$z2 <- rnorm(nrow(d))

Stochastic search variable selection

Under varsel = "ssvs" each candidate coefficient carries a mixture of two normal priors centred on zero: a tight one of standard deviation τ0\tau_0 standing for the regressor being absent from the frontier, and a loose one of τ1>τ0\tau_1 > \tau_0 standing for its being present. The indicator says which of the two is in force in that sweep. The regressor never leaves the design matrix, and an excluded coefficient is held near zero rather than at it.

The two standard deviations can be given directly as tau, or derived with semiautomatic, which multiplies the least squares standard error of each coefficient by the two factors supplied. The second is the one to reach for when the regressors sit on scales that differ, since the prior then follows the scale of each coefficient instead of being the same for all of them.

ssvs <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = d, varsel = "ssvs",
                           iterations = 4000, burnin = 1000)
ssvs <- add_priors(ssvs, varsel = list(semiautomatic = c(0.1, 10)))
ssvs <- add_posterior_coefficients(add_seed(ssvs, 1234))

summary(ssvs)
#> Bayesian stochastic frontier model
#> 
#> Call:
#> create_sfmodel_exp(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = d, 
#>     varsel = "ssvs", iterations = 4000, burnin = 1000)
#> 
#> Frontier:           production
#> Variable selection: SSVS
#> Inefficiency:       exponential
#> Observations:       400
#> Units:              400
#> Draws:              4000 after 1000 burn-in, thinning 1
#> 
#> Posterior summary, 95% credible bands:
#>                mean     sd    2.5%  median  97.5%    PIP  ESS
#> (Intercept)  0.9711 0.0262  0.9163  0.9718 1.0224     NA  188
#> x1           0.5023 0.0141  0.4738  0.5023 0.5300 1.0000 1958
#> x2           0.3058 0.0144  0.2781  0.3060 0.3344 1.0000 1954
#> z1           0.0014 0.0064 -0.0040  0.0002 0.0215 0.1215  733
#> z2          -0.0035 0.0097 -0.0358 -0.0004 0.0033 0.1820  268
#> sigma_v      0.2287 0.0160  0.1989  0.2278 0.2616     NA  217
#> lambda       4.9250 0.6631  3.8579  4.8291 6.4961     NA  168
#> 
#> Posterior mean efficiency, per observation:
#>   mean    min median    max 
#> 0.8295 0.3283 0.8573 0.9489

The PIP column is the share of draws in which the regressor was in the frontier. The two that generated the data are kept throughout; the two that did not are excluded in most sweeps.

The intercept is NA because it was never a candidate. It is the level of the frontier rather than the effect of a regressor, so selecting it away would move every efficiency score instead of dropping a variable, and it is left out by default. exclude_intercept = FALSE puts it in.

Bayesian variable selection

Under varsel = "bvs" the indicator multiplies the regressor rather than its prior. The frontier is xi′Λβx_i' \Lambda \beta with Λ\Lambda the diagonal matrix of indicators, so an excluded regressor leaves the likelihood outright and the coefficient stored for it is an exact zero.

There is no mixture here and so no pair of standard deviations to elicit. The coefficient keeps the ordinary normal prior of coef, and the only thing varsel needs is inprior.

bvs <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = d, varsel = "bvs",
                          iterations = 4000, burnin = 1000)
bvs <- add_priors(bvs, coef = list(mu = 0, v_i = 1),
                  varsel = list(inprior = 0.5))
bvs <- add_posterior_coefficients(add_seed(bvs, 1234))

summary(bvs)
#> Bayesian stochastic frontier model
#> 
#> Call:
#> create_sfmodel_exp(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = d, 
#>     varsel = "bvs", iterations = 4000, burnin = 1000)
#> 
#> Frontier:           production
#> Variable selection: BVS
#> Inefficiency:       exponential
#> Observations:       400
#> Units:              400
#> Draws:              4000 after 1000 burn-in, thinning 1
#> 
#> Posterior summary, 95% credible bands:
#>                mean     sd    2.5% median  97.5%   PIP  ESS
#> (Intercept)  0.9728 0.0262  0.9191 0.9734 1.0235    NA  216
#> x1           0.5068 0.0142  0.4799 0.5067 0.5346 1.000 1883
#> x2           0.3084 0.0142  0.2811 0.3084 0.3367 1.000 1979
#> z1           0.0002 0.0026  0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 0.016 1201
#> z2          -0.0010 0.0053 -0.0201 0.0000 0.0000 0.053  376
#> sigma_v      0.2281 0.0159  0.1986 0.2275 0.2600    NA  318
#> lambda       4.8773 0.6297  3.8691 4.8024 6.3269    NA  190
#> 
#> Posterior mean efficiency, per observation:
#>   mean    min median    max 
#> 0.8283 0.3233 0.8573 0.9485

The zeros are literal, and they line up with the indicators exactly:

beta <- as.matrix(bvs$posterior$beta$coeffs)
inclusion <- as.matrix(bvs$posterior$inclusion$coeffs)

round(colMeans(beta == 0), 3)
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2          z1          z2 
#>       0.000       0.000       0.000       0.984       0.947
round(1 - colMeans(inclusion), 3)
#>    x1    x2    z1    z2 
#> 0.000 0.000 0.984 0.947

This is what coef() and fitted() then work from: the coefficient a sweep built its frontier with, zero included, so the posterior mean of a coefficient is its effect averaged over the frontiers the selection admitted.

How to read a PIP

A low PIP does not mean the coefficient is small; it means the regressor was usually not in the model. The mean and the credible band on the same row are averages over both states of the indicator, which is why a coefficient with a low PIP has a posterior concentrated near zero rather than one centred on its least squares value:

round(quantile(as.matrix(ssvs$posterior$beta$coeffs)[, "z1"],
               c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)), 4)
#>      5%     50%     95% 
#> -0.0029  0.0002  0.0138
round(coef(lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = d))[["z1"]], 4)
#> [1] 0.0134

This is model averaging rather than model choice. Nothing has been removed from the object, and there is no single selected model to report. If a single frontier is wanted at the end, the usual convention is to keep the regressors whose PIP exceeds one half and refit without the selection, and to say that that is what was done.

The prior that Bayesian variable selection needs

The two algorithms part company over what happens to an excluded coefficient, and this is the practical difference between them.

Under SSVS an excluded coefficient is held at zero by the tight half of its own prior, so it is always within reach of being included again. Under BVS it is absent from the likelihood altogether, and the sweep draws it from the prior in coef. The wider that prior, the further the coefficient wanders while it is out, and a coefficient that has wandered far from anything the data support is one the likelihood will not admit back.

The effect is not subtle. Below, the same model is fitted at five prior widths. What matters is not the width itself but the width relative to the scale of the coefficient, so it is reported as a multiple of the least squares standard error, which is the scale add_priors() measures against too.

se <- coef(summary(lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1, data = d)))["z1", "Std. Error"]

run <- function(v_i) {
  m <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1, data = d, varsel = "bvs",
                          iterations = 2000, burnin = 1000)
  m <- suppressWarnings(
    add_priors(m, coef = list(mu = 0, v_i = v_i),
               varsel = list(inprior = 0.5)))
  m <- add_posterior_coefficients(add_seed(m, 42))
  z1 <- as.matrix(m$posterior$inclusion$coeffs)[, "z1"]
  data.frame(prior_sd = round(1 / sqrt(v_i), 3),
             multiple_of_se = round((1 / sqrt(v_i)) / se),
             switches = sum(diff(z1) != 0),
             pip_z1 = mean(z1))
}

do.call(rbind, lapply(c(100, 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01), run))
#>   prior_sd multiple_of_se switches pip_z1
#> 1    0.100              6      320 0.1525
#> 2    0.316             20      128 0.0790
#> 3    1.000             64       29 0.0180
#> 4    3.162            201        4 0.0025
#> 5   10.000            636        2 0.0015

Past a couple of hundred times the standard error the indicator never changes state for the whole run. The posterior inclusion probability of exactly zero that comes back is not a finding about z1; it is a chain that started outside the model and never got back in. add_priors() measures that ratio and warns above a hundred:

bad <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1, data = d, varsel = "bvs",
                          iterations = 100, burnin = 100)
bad <- tryCatch(add_priors(bad, varsel = list(inprior = 0.5)),
                warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
writeLines(strwrap(bad, 72))
#> The prior on x1, x2, z1 is too wide for the Bayesian variable selection
#> to move: its standard deviation is 658 times the least squares standard
#> error of the coefficient, so a sweep that excludes the regressor draws
#> a coefficient the likelihood will not admit back, and the indicator is
#> likely to stay where it started for the whole run. Give 'coef$v_i' a
#> precision of the order of the inverse squared scale of the coefficient,
#> or use varsel = "ssvs", which does not have to travel between the prior
#> and the data to change state.

The package default for coef$v_i is 0.01, which is past the bound, so a BVS model that does not set coef$v_i will say so. A prior precision of zero, the flat limiting prior the package otherwise allows, is refused outright: there would be nothing to draw an excluded coefficient from.

Note also the column of inclusion probabilities in the table above. Even over the range where the chain mixes, the probability falls as the prior widens, from 0.17 to 0.03. That is Bartlett’s paradox: the Bayes factor between the two states depends on how spread out the prior on the coefficient is, and a prior made vaguer penalises the larger model. It is a property of the algorithm, not of this implementation, and it is the reason to report a BVS inclusion probability together with the prior that produced it.

Which of the two

"ssvs" "bvs"
Excluded coefficient held near zero by a tight prior exactly zero
What the prior does the two-point mixture in varsel the ordinary normal in coef
Needs a proper coef$v_i no yes, and on the scale of the data
Mixing under correlated regressors better worse
Sensitivity to the prior width mild Bartlett’s paradox

SSVS is the safer choice when the prior was not picked with the selection in mind, and the better one when the regressors are correlated, since nothing has to travel between the prior and the data to change state. BVS gives exact zeros, a frontier that genuinely omits a regressor, and an indicator that needs no threshold to interpret.

Where the answer matters, run both. They agree here:

rbind(ssvs = round(colMeans(as.matrix(ssvs$posterior$inclusion$coeffs)), 3),
      bvs = round(colMeans(as.matrix(bvs$posterior$inclusion$coeffs)), 3))
#>      x1 x2    z1    z2
#> ssvs  1  1 0.122 0.182
#> bvs   1  1 0.016 0.053

Choosing the candidates

Both algorithms take the same three arguments for this. include names the columns of the design matrix to select on, by name or by position; exclude_intercept drops the intercept from whatever that leaves, which it does by default; and inprior sets the prior inclusion probability, either one number or one per candidate.

picked <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = d,
                             varsel = "ssvs", iterations = 1000,
                             burnin = 500)
picked <- add_priors(picked,
                     varsel = list(tau = c(0.01, 10),
                                   include = c("z1", "z2"),
                                   inprior = 0.2))
picked$priors$varsel$names
#> [1] "z1" "z2"

A regressor the frontier is known to need should be left out of the selection rather than given a high inprior: the first states the knowledge, the second only tilts the search.

What the selection does not touch

Variable selection applies to the frontier. The inefficiency term, the error and the augmented draws are sampled exactly as they are without it, so the efficiency scores are read off the draws in the usual way, with the one difference that they are now averaged over the frontiers the selection admits rather than conditioned on one:

plain <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1 + z2, data = d,
                            iterations = 4000, burnin = 1000)
plain <- add_posterior_coefficients(add_priors(add_seed(plain, 1234)))

round(c(none = mean(efficiency(plain)$mean),
        ssvs = mean(efficiency(ssvs)$mean),
        bvs = mean(efficiency(bvs)$mean)), 4)
#>   none   ssvs    bvs 
#> 0.8313 0.8295 0.8283

The scores barely move, which is what to expect when the regressors being dropped were noise: they were contributing nothing to the frontier, so removing them takes nothing away from it. The gain is in the coefficients and in not having had to decide by hand.

The four-component model

varsel sits in the same place in create_sfmodel4_exp() and create_sfmodel4_hn(), and means the same thing. The selection is on the frontier, so the unit effect and the two one-sided terms are untouched by it.

dp <- sim_sf4(n = 50, n_time = 8, beta = c(1, 0.5, 0.3))
dp$z1 <- rnorm(nrow(dp))

m4 <- create_sfmodel4_exp(y ~ x1 + x2 + z1, data = dp, id = "id",
                          varsel = "ssvs", iterations = 2000, burnin = 1000)
m4 <- add_priors(m4, varsel = list(semiautomatic = c(0.1, 10)))
m4 <- add_posterior_coefficients(add_seed(m4, 1234))

round(colMeans(as.matrix(m4$posterior$inclusion$coeffs)), 3)
#>   x1   x2   z1 
#> 1.00 1.00 0.07

Information criteria

selection_criteria() works as it always does, with one caveat. AIC, BIC and HQ charge the model for every coefficient the frontier was written with, not for the number the selection kept, because that number is not the same in every draw and there is no whole number to subtract. WAIC reads the effective number of parameters off the draws and accounts for the selection by itself, so it is the one to compare a selected model with an unselected one on.

crit <- function(m) selection_criteria(add_posterior_loglik(m))
round(c(none = crit(plain)$WAIC$mean, ssvs = crit(ssvs)$WAIC$mean,
        bvs = crit(bvs)$WAIC$mean), 2)
#>   none   ssvs    bvs 
#> 180.43 179.02 178.28

George, E. I., Sun, D., & Ni, S. (2008). Bayesian stochastic search for VAR model restrictions. Journal of Econometrics, 142(1), 553–580.

Korobilis, D. (2013). VAR forecasting using Bayesian variable selection. Journal of Applied Econometrics, 28(2), 204–230.

van den Broeck, J., Koop, G., Osiewalski, J., & Steel, M. F. J. (1994). Stochastic frontier models: A Bayesian perspective. Journal of Econometrics, 61(2), 273–303.
